analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law shielding gun makers and dealers from most lawsuits by shooting victims.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would let victims sue gun makers and dealers, was introduced in the Senate in June 2025 with 27 Democratic and Independent cosponsors and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2005, a federal law has generally blocked victims of gun violence from suing gun manufacturers, sellers, and dealers for damages caused by the criminal misuse of a firearm. This bill would repeal that shield and also allow government gun-trace data to be used as evidence in civil lawsuits. It has 27 cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents, and has been referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee with no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gun violence and their families, who could sue firearm manufacturers, sellers, dealers, and trade associations over how a gun used in a crime was made, marketed, or sold. It also helps state and local governments pursuing such claims, since trace data showing where crime guns came from could be used in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun violence victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the federal law that blocks civil lawsuits against firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for harms from criminal or unlawful misuse of a gun.
It makes ATF firearms trace data discoverable and admissible as evidence in civil suits and administrative proceedings, so victims can use government data showing how guns reached the street.

analysis.who_pays: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, importers, dealers, and trade associations, which would face civil lawsuits and the cost of defending them; some of that cost could be passed to gun buyers through prices or insurance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and trade associations

drawbacks.text: Repealing the shield exposes lawful gun makers and sellers to lawsuits over how third parties criminally misuse their products, a cost opponents say could burden or close domestic firearms businesses and raise prices for lawful buyers.

Opening the ATF firearms trace database to discovery in civil cases would put sensitive law-enforcement trace information in the hands of litigants nationwide, raising concerns about how that data is used outside its original investigative purpose.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is meaningful: it would restore a standard legal remedy that families currently lack and let courts see government trace data when gun-industry practices are at issue. The costs are real but contested: gun makers and dealers would face open-ended litigation exposure from the criminal misuse of their products, which the industry argues could drive firms out of business or raise prices, and opponents argue liability should rest with the person who pulled the trigger. The bill is a straightforward repeal rather than a carefully tailored liability rule, so its litigation consequences would unfold case by case.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on June 4, 2025, and has received no hearing, no vote, and no further action since.

narrative.text: The bill's only recorded action since introduction is its referral to the Judiciary Committee on June 4, 2025.
All 27 cosponsors are Democrats or Independents; no Republican has signed on.
The bill would repeal the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, the 2005 law that shields the gun industry from most civil suits over criminal misuse of firearms.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The gun industry, which keeps the liability shield as long as the bill goes nowhere, and the congressional majority that has no need to act on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The gun industry keeps its liability shield

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 26 cosponsors.

for.name: 27 Senate Democrats and Independents
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sen. Schumer (Minority Leader) and Sen. Durbin (Judiciary ranking member)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members of the Judiciary Committee itself.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controls the Senate agenda and committee throughput; has taken no action to advance the bill, which remains without a hearing or vote.

against.name: National Rifle Association and firearms industry groups
against.what_they_did: Longstanding and vocal defenders of the liability shield the bill would repeal, opposing its repeal in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors are Democrats or Independents; no Republican has joined, and with Republicans holding the Senate majority the bill faces no path to a vote.

industries.industry: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers and dealers
industries.note: The bill repeals the federal shield that has protected the gun industry from most civil suits since 2005, exposing manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations to negligence and other liability claims over criminal misuse of their products, and lets plaintiffs use ATF trace data against them in court. Gun companies' interest runs against victims seeking compensation.

Trade associations are currently named plaintiffs-defendants shielded by the PLCAA; the bill strips that protection, making them directly suable. Their stake is opposite to that of gun-violence victims.
Repeal would generate substantial new litigation, creating work and risk for insurers and plaintiffs' and defense attorneys. The effect on ordinary people runs through whether victims' suits succeed.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and Republicans controlling the Senate agenda, the bill will almost certainly remain in the Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote for the rest of this Congress, as similar repeal attempts have in past Congresses.
